name: Quatro de Fevereiro International Airport
before:
Read this one before quoting anything into Luanda. The airport closed to all commercial flights on 1 March 2026.

Quatro de Fevereiro was the old international airport for Luanda, in the southern part of the city, handling about 5.6 million passengers in 2018. All airline operations moved in March 2026 to the new Dr. António Agostinho Neto International Airport, 40 km south of Luanda, so any itinerary, transfer time or hotel distance based on the old airport is now wrong.

For background, the airport was built from 1951 and opened in 1954 as Aeroporto Presidente Craveiro Lopes, after the Portuguese president who inaugurated it. In August, September and October 1975 it was the scene of Operation Air Bridge, when tens of thousands of Portuguese Angolans camped at the airport waiting for evacuation flights to Lisbon in the weeks before independence. It was renamed in 1976 after 4 February, the national holiday marking the start of the armed struggle against Portuguese rule in 1961.
after:
Read this one before quoting anything into Luanda. Its scheduled passenger flights have moved to the new Dr. António Agostinho Neto International Airport (NBJ), about 40 km from central Luanda, in a transfer completed on 1 March 2026.

Quatro de Fevereiro, in the south of the city, was the old international airport for Luanda. The move away from it began in November 2024, and any itinerary, transfer time or hotel distance based on the old airport is now wrong.

For background, building began in 1951 and the airport opened in 1954, named after Craveiro Lopes, the Portuguese president who inaugurated it. In 1975, before independence, Portuguese Angolans camped at the airport waiting for evacuation flights to Lisbon. It was renamed in 1976 after 4 February 1961, the start of the armed struggle against Portuguese rule.

claims.claim: scheduled passenger flights have moved to the new airport
claims.inAfter: Its scheduled passenger flights have moved
claims.note: Was 'closed to all commercial flights'. Both Angolan reports, quoting the new airport's temporary operator (ATO), speak of 'regular' passenger flights ('voos regulares', the Portuguese term for scheduled services). The old airport is not closed: ANGOP (10 Nov 2023) reported the government's plan to keep it for special, executive (presidential), non-commercial and non-scheduled flights, and FlightAware on 23 Sep 2026 still shows daily movements there, with its 'Scheduled' lists empty. So the text says what moved and no more.

claims.claim: about 40 km from central Luanda
claims.note: Was '40 km south of Luanda'. The distance has two sources; the direction does not. Airlink puts the new airport 'approximately 45km East' of the city, against Wikipedia's 'south'. As a cross-check only (not a source), OurAirports' position for FNBJ is 37.6 km in a straight line from the GeoNames centre of Luanda at 129 degrees, which is south east, so 'about 40 km' holds and neither written direction does. The direction is cut. Airlink's 45 km is probably the road distance; it is not quoted.

claims.claim: 1975: Portuguese Angolans camped at the airport before independence, waiting for evacuation flights to Lisbon
claims.inAfter: In 1975, before independence, Portuguese Angolans camped at the airport waiting for evacuation flights to Lisbon.
claims.note: Good sources disagree on the scale: Wikipedia says tens of thousands, Buala says half a million ('meio milhão'), so no number is given. Buala calls them Portuguese settlers, most of whom had never been to Portugal, which fits 'Portuguese Angolans'. The months and the name Operation Air Bridge are Wikipedia's alone and are cut. Buala's essay cites Peralta, The Retornados and the Ending of Empire in Angola (Hurst, 2022), not Wikipedia.

sources.quote: 1975 the airport hosted tens of thousands of mostly white Portuguese Angolans fleeing to Lisbon (during Operation Air Bridge) who camped out while awaiting evacuation flights during the weeks before Angola's Independence.

claims.claim: closed to all commercial flights on 1 March 2026
claims.wasBefore: The airport closed to all commercial flights on 1 March 2026.
claims.why: Overstated. The two Angolan reports say the transfer of regular (scheduled) passenger flights was completed that day; the 2023 government plan keeps non-scheduled, executive and non-commercial flights at the old airport, and FlightAware still shows movements there on 23 Sep 2026. Replaced by the scheduled passenger flights claim.

claims.claim: about 5.6 million passengers in 2018
claims.why: A 2018 figure for an airport that has since lost its scheduled flights, and no second source.

claims.claim: all airline operations moved in March 2026
claims.wasBefore: All airline operations moved in March 2026
claims.why: Wrong in two ways: the move ran from November 2024 and only finished on 1 March 2026, and it covered scheduled passenger flights, not every operation. Replaced by the start and completion dates.

claims.claim: the new airport is south of Luanda
claims.why: Direction disputed: Wikipedia says south, Airlink says east, and the coordinates put it south east. The distance is kept with two sources.

claims.claim: first named Aeroporto Presidente Craveiro Lopes
claims.why: The exact name is only in Wikipedia and in a Vida Económica column that borrows from Wikipedia elsewhere; HPIP, the heritage source Wikipedia cites, would not load (502 and 503), and the archived copy is blocked here. ANGOP and Buala confirm only that it was first named after him, which is kept.

claims.claim: August to October 1975, Operation Air Bridge
claims.wasBefore: In August, September and October 1975 it was the scene of Operation Air Bridge
claims.why: The months and the operation's English name are Wikipedia's alone. The New York Times and The Economist reports it cites are blocked in this session.

claims.claim: tens of thousands camped at the airport
claims.wasBefore: when tens of thousands of Portuguese Angolans
claims.why: Good sources disagree on the scale (tens of thousands against half a million), so no number is given.

claims.claim: in the weeks before independence
claims.why: Softened to 'before independence'. Buala puts it on the brink of independence and gives no timescale.

claims.wasBefore: the national holiday marking the start of the armed struggle
claims.why: Only Wikipedia calls it a national holiday. ANGOP confirms the date and what it marks, which is kept.
